Answer ALL questions: Section A is Pure Mathematics (questions 1 to 35) and Section B is Statistics (questions 36 to 50). Mathematical tables (formulae booklets) and calculators are allowed. Each question has FOUR suggested answers A, B, C and D; mark only one answer for each question (if you mark more than one answer you score zero). Avoid spending too much time on any one question. Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION A: PURE MATHEMATICS**

$\dfrac{5x+1}{(x-1)(x+2)}\equiv$
questions.corrige_markdown: Write $\dfrac{5x+1}{(x-1)(x+2)}\equiv\dfrac{A}{x-1}+\dfrac{B}{x+2}$, so $5x+1\equiv A(x+2)+B(x-1)$. Put $x=1$: $6=3A$, so $A=2$. Put $x=-2$: $-9=-3B$, so $B=3$. Hence the expression is $\dfrac{2}{x-1}+\dfrac{3}{x+2}$. Check at $x=0$: left side $\dfrac{1}{(-1)(2)}=-\dfrac12$; right side $-2+\dfrac32=-\dfrac12$. Option A has the two numerators swapped (at $x=0$ it gives $-2$, not $-\tfrac12$). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The equations of the vertical asymptotes to the graph of $f(x)=\dfrac{4}{x^2-1}$ are
questions.corrige_markdown: Vertical asymptotes occur where the denominator is zero and the numerator is not. $x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1)=0$ gives $x=1$ and $x=-1$, and the numerator $4$ is never zero, so both lines are vertical asymptotes (the horizontal asymptote is $y=0$). The values $4$ and $-4$ in the other options are not roots of $x^2-1$: the numerator $4$ plays no part in locating vertical asymptotes. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Two functions $f$ and $g$ are defined by $f(x)=2x+3$ and $g(x)=x-2$. The composite function $(g\circ f)$ is given by
questions.corrige_markdown: $(g\circ f)(x)=g\big(f(x)\big)$: apply $f$ first, then $g$. $g(2x+3)=(2x+3)-2=2x+1$. Option B is the other composite, $(f\circ g)(x)=f(x-2)=2(x-2)+3=2x-1$, which applies the functions in the wrong order. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\4&5&6\\7&8&9\end{pmatrix}$, then the cofactor of the element $6$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The cofactor of the entry in row $i$, column $j$ is $C_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}M_{ij}$, where the minor $M_{ij}$ is the determinant left after deleting row $i$ and column $j$. The element $6$ is in row $2$, column $3$, so the sign is $(-1)^{2+3}=-1$. Deleting row $2$ and column $3$ leaves $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\7&8\end{pmatrix}$, so $C_{23}=-\begin{vmatrix}1&2\\7&8\end{vmatrix}=-(8-14)=6$. Option B is the minor without its sign; options C and D change the entries of the minor, which come directly from the matrix. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $4^{2-x}=4\left(2^{1-x}\right)$, the value of $x$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Write everything in base $2$. Left side: $4^{2-x}=(2^2)^{2-x}=2^{4-2x}$. Right side: $4\cdot2^{1-x}=2^2\cdot2^{1-x}=2^{3-x}$. Equating exponents, $4-2x=3-x$, so $x=1$. Check: $4^{1}=4$ and $4\cdot2^{0}=4$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $\ln(x+6)+\ln 9=\ln(x+7)+\ln 6$, the value of $x$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Combine each side with $\ln a+\ln b=\ln(ab)$: $\ln\big(9(x+6)\big)=\ln\big(6(x+7)\big)$. Since $\ln$ is one-to-one, $9x+54=6x+42$, so $3x=-12$ and $x=-4$. Both logarithms $\ln(x+6)=\ln2$ and $\ln(x+7)=\ln3$ are defined, so $x=-4$ is admissible. Check: $\ln2+\ln9=\ln18$ and $\ln3+\ln6=\ln18$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If the roots of the quadratic equation $px^2-qx-r=0$ are real, then
questions.corrige_markdown: For $ax^2+bx+c=0$ the roots are real when the discriminant $b^2-4ac\ge0$. Here $a=p$, $b=-q$, $c=-r$, so $b^2-4ac=q^2-4(p)(-r)=q^2+4pr$. Real roots (equal roots allowed) need $q^2+4pr\ge0$. Options A and D forget that $c=-r$; options C and D use a strict inequality, which would mean two distinct real roots. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1+\dfrac{2}{3n}\right)^{n}=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Use the standard limit $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1+\dfrac{c}{n}\right)^{n}=e^{c}$ with $c=\dfrac23$. Equivalently put $m=\dfrac{3n}{2}$, so $n=\dfrac{2m}{3}$ and $\left(1+\dfrac1m\right)^{2m/3}=\left[\left(1+\dfrac1m\right)^{m}\right]^{2/3}\to e^{2/3}$. Option A is the reciprocal exponent, from putting $n=\dfrac{3m}{2}$ by mistake. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given two statements $p$ and $q$, the converse of $p\Rightarrow q$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The converse of an implication swaps hypothesis and conclusion: the converse of $p\Rightarrow q$ is $q\Rightarrow p$. The statement $\sim p\Rightarrow\sim q$ would be the inverse, and $\sim q\Rightarrow\sim p$ the contrapositive (logically equivalent to the original, so not its converse). **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The solution of the simultaneous equations $2x+3y=1$, $3x-y=7$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: From the second equation $y=3x-7$. Substitute in the first: $2x+3(3x-7)=1$, so $11x-21=1$, $x=2$ and $y=3(2)-7=-1$. Check: $2(2)+3(-1)=1$ and $3(2)-(-1)=7$. Options A, B and C each fail at least one equation (for example $(2,1)$ gives $2x+3y=7\ne1$). **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{1-\cos x}{x}=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Both numerator and denominator tend to $0$. By l'Hospital's rule, $\lim\dfrac{\sin x}{1}=0$. Alternatively $1-\cos x\approx\dfrac{x^2}{2}$ for small $x$, so the quotient behaves like $\dfrac{x}{2}\to0$. The values $1$ and $\dfrac12$ belong to $\dfrac{\sin x}{x}$ and $\dfrac{1-\cos x}{x^2}$, which are different limits. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Using the substitution $u=1+x^2$, $\displaystyle\int_0^1 2x(1+x^2)^3\,dx=$
questions.corrige_markdown: With $u=1+x^2$, $du=2x\,dx$; when $x=0$, $u=1$ and when $x=1$, $u=2$. So $\displaystyle\int_0^1 2x(1+x^2)^3\,dx=\int_1^2u^3\,du=\left[\dfrac{u^4}{4}\right]_1^2=\dfrac{16}{4}-\dfrac14=\dfrac{15}{4}$. Check by expanding: $2x(1+3x^2+3x^4+x^6)$ integrates to $x^2+\tfrac32x^4+x^6+\tfrac14x^8$, which equals $1+1.5+1+0.25$ at $x=1$, that is $3.75$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{2x+1}{2x}\,dx=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Split the fraction: $\dfrac{2x+1}{2x}=1+\dfrac{1}{2x}$. Then $\displaystyle\int\left(1+\dfrac{1}{2x}\right)dx=x+\dfrac12\ln|x|+K$. Differentiating the result gives $1+\dfrac{1}{2x}$, as required. Options C and D lose the factor $\dfrac12$ (they would differentiate to $1+\dfrac2x$), and option B integrates $\dfrac1x$ as a power. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Using De Moivre's theorem, the complex number $(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)^5$ is equal to
questions.corrige_markdown: De Moivre's theorem states $(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)^n=\cos n\theta+i\sin n\theta$ for integer $n$. With $n=5$: $\cos5\theta+i\sin5\theta$ (the modulus stays $1$ and the argument is multiplied by $5$). Option D is the fifth root rule with $n=\dfrac15$ and option A raises the angle instead of multiplying it. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ are coplanar vectors, where $\mathbf u=2\mathbf i-\mathbf j+6\mathbf k$ and $\mathbf v=-3\mathbf i+5\mathbf j+\mathbf k$, $\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=$
questions.corrige_markdown: $\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\2&-1&6\\-3&5&1\end{vmatrix}=\big((-1)(1)-(6)(5)\big)\mathbf i-\big((2)(1)-(6)(-3)\big)\mathbf j+\big((2)(5)-(-1)(-3)\big)\mathbf k=-31\mathbf i-20\mathbf j+7\mathbf k$. Check: the result must be perpendicular to both vectors: $\mathbf u\cdot(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v)=-62+20+42=0$ and $\mathbf v\cdot(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v)=93-100+7=0$. Options B, C and D differ from the correct vector by sign errors in one or more components. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A function $f$ is continuous on the interval $[a,b]$ and differentiable in the interval $(a,b)$. The mean value theorem states that there exists a value $c$, $a<c<b$, such that
questions.corrige_markdown: The mean value theorem says that somewhere strictly between $a$ and $b$ the tangent is parallel to the chord joining $(a,f(a))$ and $(b,f(b))$, so $f'(c)=\dfrac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$, the gradient of the chord. Option A adds the function values, and options C and D use values of $f'$ at the end points, which is not what the theorem involves. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The tangent of the acute angle between the lines $y=4x-3$ and $y=x-2$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The gradients are $m_1=4$ and $m_2=1$. For the angle $\phi$ between two lines, $\tan\phi=\left|\dfrac{m_1-m_2}{1+m_1m_2}\right|=\dfrac{3}{1+4}=\dfrac35$, which is positive because the angle is acute. A negative value would correspond to the obtuse angle $180^\circ-\phi$, and $\dfrac53$ is the reciprocal, obtained by inverting the formula. Check: $\arctan4-\arctan1\approx75.96^\circ-45^\circ=30.96^\circ$ and $\tan30.96^\circ=0.6$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The general solution of the differential equation $3\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{x^2}+x$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The equation is $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac13\left(x^{-2}+x\right)$, which integrates directly: $y=\dfrac13\left(\dfrac{x^{-1}}{-1}+\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right)+c=\dfrac13\left(\dfrac{x^2}{2}-\dfrac1x\right)+c$. Check by differentiating: $\dfrac13\left(x+\dfrac1{x^2}\right)$, so $3\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x+\dfrac1{x^2}$. Option B has the wrong sign on $\dfrac1x$ (the integral of $x^{-2}$ is $-x^{-1}$). **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A geometric progression has first term $16$ and sum to infinity $40$. The common ratio of the progression is
questions.corrige_markdown: For $|r|<1$, $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$. So $\dfrac{16}{1-r}=40$, giving $1-r=\dfrac{16}{40}=\dfrac25$ and $r=\dfrac35$. Check: $\dfrac{16}{1-0.6}=\dfrac{16}{0.4}=40$. Option A is the value of $1-r$, not $r$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The equation of a line is $\mathbf r=\mathbf i-3\mathbf j+7\mathbf k+\mu(3\mathbf i+\mathbf j+2\mathbf k)$ and the equation of a plane is $2x+3y-2z=5$. The sine of the acute angle between the line and the plane is

*Options as printed:* A) $\dfrac27$   B) $\dfrac37$   C) $\dfrac17$   D) $\dfrac57$
questions.corrige_markdown:
The direction of the line is $\mathbf d=3\mathbf i+\mathbf j+2\mathbf k$ and a normal to the plane is $\mathbf n=2\mathbf i+3\mathbf j-2\mathbf k$. The angle $\varphi$ between a line and a plane satisfies $\sin\varphi=\dfrac{|\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf d||\mathbf n|}$. Here $\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n=6+3-4=5$, $|\mathbf d|=\sqrt{14}$ and $|\mathbf n|=\sqrt{17}$, so $\sin\varphi=\dfrac{5}{\sqrt{238}}\approx0.324$ ($\varphi\approx18.9^\circ$). **Answer: $\sin\varphi=\dfrac{5}{\sqrt{238}}$.** This value is none of the printed options ($\frac27\approx0.286$, $\frac37\approx0.429$, $\frac17\approx0.143$, $\frac57\approx0.714$), so the printed question is inconsistent (misprinted data or options).



The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The solution set of $\dfrac{x+1}{x}\geq2$ is

*Options as printed:* A) $\{x: 0\ \square\ x\le-1\ \text{or}\ x\ge\ \square\}$ (printed illegibly in the scan)   B) $\{x: x\le0\ \text{or}\ x\ge1\}$   C) $\{x:-1\le x\le0\}$   D) $\{x: x\ge-1\}$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Move everything to one side: $\dfrac{x+1}{x}-2\ge0\iff\dfrac{x+1-2x}{x}\ge0\iff\dfrac{1-x}{x}\ge0$. The quotient $\dfrac{1-x}{x}$ changes sign at $x=0$ (undefined there) and at $x=1$. Sign table: for $x<0$ the numerator $1-x>0$ and the denominator $x<0$, so the quotient is negative; for $0<x<1$ both are positive, so the quotient is positive; for $x>1$ the numerator is negative and the denominator positive, so the quotient is negative. At $x=1$ the quotient is $0$, which satisfies $\ge0$; $x=0$ must be excluded. Hence the solution set is $\{x:0<x\le1\}=(0,1]$. Check: $x=\tfrac12$ gives $3\ge2$ (true), $x=1$ gives $2\ge2$ (true), $x=2$ gives $1.5\ge2$ (false), $x=-1$ gives $0\ge2$ (false). This set is not among the legible options (option B, $x\le0$ or $x\ge1$, is false at $x=2$ and undefined at $x=0$; options C and D are false at $x=-1$), and option A is garbled in the scan.

**Answer: $\{x:0<x\le1\}$ (not among the legible options).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $4\cos\theta+3\sin\theta\equiv R\sin(\theta+\alpha)$, the value of $R$ and $\tan\alpha$ respectively are
questions.corrige_markdown: Expand $R\sin(\theta+\alpha)=R\cos\alpha\,\sin\theta+R\sin\alpha\,\cos\theta$ and compare with $3\sin\theta+4\cos\theta$: $R\cos\alpha=3$ and $R\sin\alpha=4$. Then $R^2=3^2+4^2=25$, so $R=5$ (the positive root), and $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{R\sin\alpha}{R\cos\alpha}=\dfrac43$ ($\alpha\approx53.13^\circ$). Options A and C give $R^2$ instead of $R$; options A and B swap the roles of sine and cosine and give $\tan\alpha=\dfrac34$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A circle with radius $4$ has its centre at the point $(2,4)$. The equation of the circle is
questions.corrige_markdown: A circle with centre $(h,k)$ and radius $r$ has equation $(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2$. With $(h,k)=(2,4)$ and $r=4$: $(x-2)^2+(y-4)^2=16$. Options B and C swap the coordinates of the centre; options B and D put $4$ on the right-hand side (that is, $r$ instead of $r^2$), which would be a circle of radius $2$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The general solution of the equation $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The principal value is $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ because $\cos\dfrac\pi6=\dfrac{\sqrt3}2$. Cosine is even and has period $2\pi$, so the general solution of $\cos\theta=\cos\alpha$ is $\theta=2n\pi\pm\alpha$, $n\in\mathbb Z$: here $\theta=2n\pi\pm\dfrac\pi6$. Options C and D use the period $\pi$ (valid for $\tan\theta$, not for $\cos\theta$), and options A and C use $\dfrac\pi3$, whose cosine is $\dfrac12$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $X$ and $Y$ are two variables related by the equation $Y=aX^2+bX$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants. A suitable linear transformation for this non-linear equation is
questions.corrige_markdown: Divide both sides by $X$ ($X\ne0$): $\dfrac{Y}{X}=aX+b$. Plotting $\dfrac YX$ against $X$ gives a straight line with gradient $a$ and intercept $b$ on the $\dfrac YX$ axis, so $a$ and $b$ can be read off. Option B is only a factorisation and is not linear in any pair of variables; option C is a true identity but not linear (it contains $\ln(aX+b)$), and option D is false because a logarithm of a sum is not the sum of logarithms: $\ln(aX^2+bX)\ne\ln(aX^2)+\ln(bX)$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A partial order relation is that which is
questions.corrige_markdown: A partial order is a relation that is reflexive ($aRa$), antisymmetric ($aRb$ and $bRa$ imply $a=b$) and transitive. Example: $\le$ on $\mathbb R$, or divisibility on the positive integers. Option A (reflexive, symmetric, transitive) defines an equivalence relation, the standard distractor. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given the parametric equations $x=2\theta+\sin2\theta$, $y=1-\cos2\theta$, where $\theta$ is the parameter, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=$
questions.corrige_markdown: $\dfrac{dx}{d\theta}=2+2\cos2\theta=2(1+\cos2\theta)$ and $\dfrac{dy}{d\theta}=2\sin2\theta$. By the chain rule $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/d\theta}{dx/d\theta}=\dfrac{2\sin2\theta}{2(1+\cos2\theta)}=\dfrac{\sin2\theta}{1+\cos2\theta}$. This simplifies to $\dfrac{2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{2\cos^2\theta}=\tan\theta$, so option B ($\cot\theta$) is the reciprocal and not equal. Options A and C carry a spurious minus sign (and A also has the wrong denominator). **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $(1+ax)^{\frac12}=1+\dfrac{x}{2}+bx^2+\cdots$
questions.corrige_markdown: The binomial series gives $(1+ax)^{1/2}=1+\dfrac12(ax)+\dfrac{\frac12\left(-\frac12\right)}{2!}(ax)^2+\cdots=1+\dfrac{a}{2}x-\dfrac{a^2}{8}x^2+\cdots$. Comparing the coefficient of $x$: $\dfrac a2=\dfrac12$, so $a=1$. Then $b=-\dfrac{a^2}{8}=-\dfrac18$. Options with $a=-1$ would give a coefficient $-\dfrac12$ for $x$, and option C has the wrong coefficient $-\dfrac14$ (the factor $\dfrac{1}{2!}$ was forgotten). **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The number of arrangements of the letters of the word $ASSASSINATION$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: ASSASSINATION has $13$ letters: A appears $3$ times, S $4$ times, I $2$ times, N $2$ times, and T and O once each ($3+4+2+2+1+1=13$). Arrangements of a word with repeated letters: $\dfrac{13!}{3!\,4!\,2!\,2!}=10\,810\,800$. Option A omits the repeated N. Options C and D use $5!$ in the numerator, which does not count all $13$ positions. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that the sum of the first $n$ terms of a sequence is $S_n=n(n+2)$, the fourth term of the sequence is
questions.corrige_markdown: The $n$th term is $u_n=S_n-S_{n-1}$. So $u_4=S_4-S_3=4(6)-3(5)=24-15=9$. In general $u_n=n(n+2)-(n-1)(n+1)=2n+1$, which gives $u_4=9$ (the sequence is $3,5,7,9,\ldots$). Option A is the sum of the first four terms $S_4$, and option B is $S_3$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The polynomial $P(x)=x^3+ax^2+2x-5$ leaves the remainder $2$ when divided by $(x-1)$. The value of $a$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: By the remainder theorem the remainder on division by $(x-1)$ is $P(1)=1+a+2-5=a-2$. Setting $a-2=2$ gives $a=4$. Check: $P(x)=x^3+4x^2+2x-5$ and $P(1)=1+4+2-5=2$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{100}(r+1)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{100}(r+1)=\sum_{r=1}^{100}r+\sum_{r=1}^{100}1=\dfrac{100\cdot101}{2}+100=5050+100=5150$. Equivalently the terms are $2,3,\ldots,101$, whose sum is $\dfrac{100(2+101)}{2}=5150$. Option A forgets the $100$ added ones. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A point $P$ divides the line segment joining the points $(10,1)$ and $(5,6)$ internally in the ratio $2:3$. The coordinates of $P$ are
questions.corrige_markdown: Take $A(10,1)$ and $B(5,6)$ with $AP:PB=2:3$. The section formula gives $P=\dfrac{3A+2B}{2+3}=\left(\dfrac{3(10)+2(5)}{5},\dfrac{3(1)+2(6)}{5}\right)=\left(\dfrac{40}{5},\dfrac{15}{5}\right)=(8,3)$. Check: $P=A+\dfrac25(B-A)=(10,1)+\dfrac25(-5,5)=(8,3)$. Option C comes from applying the ratio the other way round ($3:2$). **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A periodic function $f$ is defined on $\mathbb R$, the set of real numbers by

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}x+2,&0<x\le3\\2x-13,&3<x\le5\end{cases}$$

If $f(x)=f(x+5k)$, $k\in\mathbb Z$, then $f(11)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: The relation $f(x)=f(x+5k)$ says that $f$ has period $5$, and the rule is given only on $(0,5]$. Reduce the argument into that interval: $11=1+5(2)$, so $f(11)=f(1)$. Since $0<1\le3$, the first rule applies: $f(1)=1+2=3$. Applying a rule directly at $x=11$ is the trap: $11+2=13$ (option A) or $2(11)-13=9$ (option B). **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The value of the constant $m$ for which the graph of the equation $y=m(x-2)^2+3$ passes through $(0,0)$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Substitute $x=0$, $y=0$: $0=m(0-2)^2+3=4m+3$, so $m=-\dfrac34$. Check: $y=-\dfrac34(x-2)^2+3$ at $x=0$ is $-\dfrac34\cdot4+3=0$. The parabola opens downwards (it has a maximum at $(2,3)$), consistent with a negative $m$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION B: STATISTICS**

Two events $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive if
questions.corrige_markdown: Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together, so $A\cap B=\varnothing$ and $P(A\cap B)=0$; then $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)$. Option D, $P(A\cup B)=1$, describes exhaustive events, a different notion. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $A$ and $B$ are two events such that $P(A')=\dfrac23$, $P(B)=\dfrac12$ and $P(A\cap B)=\dfrac1{12}$. The value of $P(A\cup B)$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: First $P(A)=1-P(A')=1-\dfrac23=\dfrac13$. The addition rule gives $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)=\dfrac13+\dfrac12-\dfrac1{12}=\dfrac{4+6-1}{12}=\dfrac9{12}=\dfrac34$. Using $P(A')=\dfrac23$ directly as $P(A)$ gives $\dfrac23+\dfrac12-\dfrac1{12}=\dfrac{13}{12}>1$, which is impossible; option D comes from adding the intersection instead of subtracting it. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A random variable $X$ has the following probability distribution

| $x$ | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $P(X=x)$ | 0.3 | 0.1 | 0.3 | 0.2 | 0.1 |

The value of $P(2\le x<4)$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The inequality $2\le x<4$ includes $x=2$ and $x=3$ but excludes $x=4$. So $P(2\le X<4)=P(X=2)+P(X=3)=0.1+0.3=0.4$. (The probabilities sum to $0.3+0.1+0.3+0.2+0.1=1$, so the table is valid.) Option C, $0.6$, wrongly includes $x=4$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A random variable $X$ is such that $\mathrm{Var}(X)=4$. $\mathrm{Var}(2X-5)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: For constants $a,b$: $\mathrm{Var}(aX+b)=a^2\mathrm{Var}(X)$; a shift $b$ does not change the spread. So $\mathrm{Var}(2X-5)=2^2\times4=16$. Option A applies the rule for expectation, $2(4)-5=3$, which is wrong for a variance, and option C forgets to square the $2$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $X\sim N(200,4)$, $P(197<X<205)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: With the notation $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$, $\mu=200$ and $\sigma^2=4$, so $\sigma=2$. Standardise with $Z=\dfrac{X-200}{2}$: $P(197<X<205)=P(-1.5<Z<2.5)=\Phi(2.5)-\Phi(-1.5)$. By symmetry $\Phi(-1.5)=1-\Phi(1.5)$, so the probability is $\Phi(2.5)-1+\Phi(1.5)=\Phi(2.5)+\Phi(1.5)-1\approx0.9938+0.9332-1=0.927$. Options A and C have the wrong sign for $\Phi(1.5)$; option B omits the $-1$ and exceeds $1$, which is impossible for a probability. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Statistics that involves collecting, organising, presenting and summarising of data relating to a sample or population is known as
questions.corrige_markdown: Descriptive statistics collects, organises, presents and summarises data (tables, charts, averages, measures of spread). Inferential statistics goes further and uses a sample to draw conclusions about a population (estimation, hypothesis tests). 'Population statistics' and 'sample statistics' only say where the data come from, not what is done with them. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A continuous random variable $X$ has a probability density function defined as follows, $f(x)=m(3-x)$, $1\le x\le3$. The value of $m$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The total probability is $1$: $\displaystyle\int_1^3m(3-x)\,dx=m\left[3x-\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_1^3=m\left[\left(9-\dfrac92\right)-\left(3-\dfrac12\right)\right]=m\left(\dfrac92-\dfrac52\right)=2m$. So $2m=1$ and $m=\dfrac12$. Check: $f(x)=\dfrac12(3-x)\ge0$ on $[1,3]$, and the triangle of base $2$ and height $f(1)=1$ has area $1$. Option A is the reciprocal. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: In statistical estimation, a more precise estimate is obtained when
questions.corrige_markdown: The precision of an estimate of a mean is governed by its standard error $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$ (a smaller standard error gives a narrower confidence interval). It is reduced by less variable data (small $\sigma$) and by a larger sample size. Random sampling (A) guards against bias, not imprecision; a high standard error (B) and a small sample (D) both make the estimate less precise. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: For the population $1,2,3$, the set of all possible samples of size $2$, taken with replacement, is
questions.corrige_markdown: Sampling with replacement allows the same value to be drawn twice, and the order of the draws gives different samples, so there are $3\times3=9$ ordered samples: all pairs $(a,b)$ with $a,b\in\{1,2,3\}$. Option B lists only the $3\times2=6$ samples without replacement; option D keeps only the repeated pairs and option C is a subset of two samples. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A random sample of size $5$ is drawn from a population with standard deviation $0.042$. The sample mean is found to be $5.12$. The $90\%$ confidence interval for the population mean is

*Options as printed:* A) $5.12\pm1.645\left(\dfrac{0.042}{5}\right)$   B) $5.12\pm0.042\left(\dfrac{1.645}{\sqrt5}\right)$   C) $5.12\pm0.042\left(\dfrac{1.645}{5}\right)$   D) $5.12\pm1.645\left(\dfrac{0.042}{\sqrt5}\right)$
questions.corrige_markdown:
The population standard deviation $\sigma=0.042$ is known, so the interval is $\bar x\pm z\,\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$, where $z$ leaves $5\%$ in each tail for $90\%$ confidence: $z=1.645$. With $n=5$: $5.12\pm1.645\times\dfrac{0.042}{\sqrt5}=5.12\pm0.0309$, that is $(5.089,\,5.151)$ to $3$ decimal places. Printed options B and D are algebraically identical ($0.042\times\dfrac{1.645}{\sqrt5}=1.645\times\dfrac{0.042}{\sqrt5}$) and both correct, so the key cannot be one single letter; options A and C are also identical to each other and wrong, because they divide by $n=5$ instead of $\sqrt n=\sqrt5$ (the standard error of a mean uses the square root).

**Answer: $5.12\pm1.645\left(\dfrac{0.042}{\sqrt5}\right)$, i.e. options B and D (equal) are both correct.**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: A manufacturer of a type of water pipe claims that the mean breaking strength of the pipes is $210\,\mathrm{kg}$. A sample of $300$ water pipes taken from his production gives a mean breaking strength of $200\,\mathrm{kg}$. The appropriate hypotheses to test the manufacturer's claim are
questions.corrige_markdown: The null hypothesis is the manufacturer's claim, $H_0:\mu=210$. The evidence is a sample mean of $200\,\mathrm{kg}$, below the claim, and the concern with a breaking strength is that the pipes are weaker than claimed, so the alternative is one-tailed in the lower direction: $H_1:\mu<210$. Option B points the wrong way (the data do not suggest a higher strength), and option C is not a valid alternative because $H_1$ cannot contain the equality of $H_0$. Option A (two-tailed) would only be right if the question asked whether the mean had simply changed. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A sample of size $11$ taken from a population has a variance $4$. The best estimate for the population variance is
questions.corrige_markdown: The unbiased estimate of the population variance is $s^2=\dfrac{n}{n-1}\times(\text{sample variance})$, where the sample variance has divisor $n$. Here $s^2=\dfrac{11}{10}\times4=4.40$. Option B inverts the factor ($4\times\dfrac{10}{11}=3.64$), and option C uses $\dfrac{11}{9}$ ($4.89$). **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $5$ pairs of values $(x,y)$ are such that $\sum xy=620$, $\sum x=40$ and $\sum y=60$. $\mathrm{Cov}(x,y)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: With $n=5$: $\bar x=\dfrac{40}{5}=8$ and $\bar y=\dfrac{60}{5}=12$. The covariance is $\mathrm{Cov}(x,y)=\dfrac{\sum xy}{n}-\bar x\bar y=\dfrac{620}{5}-8\times12=124-96=28$. Option B is $\dfrac{\sum xy}{n}$ alone, without subtracting $\bar x\bar y$. (With divisor $n-1$ the sample covariance would be $\dfrac{620-480}{4}=35$, which is not an option, so the divisor $n$ is the one intended.) **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The equations of the regression lines of $Y$ on $X$ and $X$ on $Y$ are, respectively, $y=2x-7$ and $x=5y-12$. The value of the product-moment correlation coefficient, $r=$

*Options as printed:* A) $-\sqrt{10}$   B) $\sqrt{10}$   C) $-\sqrt{84}$   D) $\sqrt{84}$
questions.corrige_markdown:
For regression lines $y=b_{yx}x+\dots$ ($Y$ on $X$) and $x=b_{xy}y+\dots$ ($X$ on $Y$), the product-moment correlation coefficient satisfies $r^2=b_{yx}\,b_{xy}$, with the sign of $r$ equal to the common sign of the two gradients. Here $b_{yx}=2$ and $b_{xy}=5$, so $r^2=2\times5=10$ and, both gradients being positive, the formula gives $r=+\sqrt{10}$ (option B). Option D, $\sqrt{84}$, is $\sqrt{7\times12}$, the product of the constant terms, which is not part of the formula; options A and C have the wrong sign. However, $|r|\le1$ always, and $r^2=10>1$ is impossible: the two printed equations cannot both be regression lines of the same data (a valid pair needs $b_{yx}\,b_{xy}\le1$, for instance $x=\tfrac15y+\dots$). The intended answer is therefore $\sqrt{10}$, but the question is mathematically flawed and no option is a valid correlation coefficient.

**Intended answer: B ($\sqrt{10}$), although $|r|>1$ is impossible.**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: For $6$ pairs of rankings, $\sum d^2=25$. Spearman's coefficient of rank correlation, $r_s=$
questions.corrige_markdown: $r_s=1-\dfrac{6\sum d^2}{n(n^2-1)}=1-\dfrac{6\times25}{6\times35}=1-\dfrac{25}{35}=1-\dfrac57=\dfrac27$ ($\approx0.286$). Option A is $\dfrac{25}{35}$, the fraction that must still be subtracted from $1$. **Answer: B.**
